title: f-strings and Formatting
intro: An **f-string** has an `f` before the quotes. Anything inside `{}` is worked out and dropped into the text: `f"Hi {name}"`. After a colon you can add a **format spec**: `{price:.2f}` shows 2 decimal places.

questions.prompt: Format specs control decimals (`.2f`), thousands separators (`,`) and width and alignment (`>8` right, `<8` left, `^8` centre). A **backslash** starts an escape: `\n` is a new line, `\t` a tab, `\"` a quote.
questions.exampleCode:
name = "Ana"
total = 1234.5
print(f"{name} owes {total:.2f}")
print(f"{total:,.1f}")
print(f"|{name:>6}|{name:<6}|")
print("Line one\nLine two")
questions.explanation: Inside `{}` you can write any expression, like `{total * 2}`.

questions.prompt: `name` and `score` are set. Store `{name} scored {score} points` in `message` using an f-string, then print it.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert message == f'{name} scored {score} points', 'message should read like: Kofi scored 92 points'

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.strip() == f'{name} scored {score} points', 'Print the message.'

questions.hint: Start with `f"`, then put each variable inside `{}`.
questions.explanation: f-strings handle numbers for you — no `str()` needed.
The value is rounded for display; `price` itself doesn't change.

questions.prompt: `width` and `height` are set. Store `Area: ` followed by their product in `report`, calculating inside the braces.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert report == f'Area: {width * height}', 'report should be Area: followed by width × height.'

questions.explanation: Any expression works inside the braces.

questions.hint: The comma in the format spec adds thousands separators.
questions.explanation: `:,` groups digits in threes with commas.

questions.prompt: `greeting` should be `Hello, Iris!` but comes out with the braces showing. Fix it.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert greeting == 'Hello, Iris!', 'greeting should be Hello, Iris!'

questions.hint: Look at the very start of the string.
questions.explanation: Without the `f`, Python treats `{name}` as ordinary characters.

questions.prompt: Fill in the format spec so `item` is **left-aligned** in a space 10 characters wide.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert line == 'tea       |', 'line should be tea followed by 7 spaces and |.'

questions.hint: `<` aligns left; the number is the width.
questions.explanation: `{item:<10}` pads `tea` with 7 spaces on the right.

questions.prompt: Build one row of a receipt table in `row`: `product` left-aligned in 10 characters, `qty` right-aligned in 3, and the line total (`qty * price`) right-aligned in 8 with 2 decimals. For example `Coffee      3    7.50`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert row == f'{product:<10}{qty:>3}{qty * price:>8.2f}', 'Check each column: <10, >3 and >8.2f.'

tests.name: width
tests.code: assert len(row) == 21, 'The row should be exactly 21 characters wide.'
tests.message: The row should be 21 characters wide.

questions.hint: Three sets of braces, each with its own spec: `<10`, `>3`, `>8.2f`.
questions.explanation: Fixed widths line columns up when you print several rows.
The backslash lets a double quote sit inside a double-quoted string.

questions.prompt: Print a summary line like `Lee: 3 items, total $47.50` using `customer`, `items` and `total` (always 2 decimals). Store it in `summary` first.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert summary == f'{customer}: {items} items, total ${total:.2f}', 'Check the wording and the 2 decimal places.'

questions.hint: The `$` is just a character before the braces; `.2f` handles the decimals.
questions.explanation: One f-string replaces several `+` joins and `str()` calls.
